item.title: Perovskite laser maintains stable performance over 400 million pulses
item.description: In a study published in Advanced Optical Materials, researchers at Vilnius University (VU) demonstrated perovskite-based laser structures that maintained stable performance over more than 400 million pulses. Their findings address one of the major challenges limiting the practical use of perovskites: their instability. These semiconductor materials could play an important role in next-generation optical technologies, but their tendency to degrade has long posed a challenge for researchers worldwide. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why the humble rabbit might be Australia's worst introduced species
item.description: The 19th-century pastoralist Thomas Austin was homesick. He yearned for the pastimes of his home in England—especially rabbit hunting. He asked his family to send him some rabbits. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Not all rattlesnakes are alike: Research suggests personality influences how rattlesnakes use their venom
item.description: Imagine encountering a rattlesnake in your backyard or while on a hike. It will most likely "freeze" to avoid attracting attention, but if it feels especially threatened, it may rattle and even strike, delivering a painful dose of venom. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Wild fish are a precious resource—here's how aquaculture can bolster food security
item.description: Small fish such as sardinella are an affordable source of protein and essential nutrients for millions of people across West Africa. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How a massive ice shelf buttressed the last ice age's glaciers—and what it could mean for Antarctica today
item.description: About 20,000 years ago, an enormous, floating ice shelf more than a mile (1.6 kilometers) thick helped lock in three of the largest ice sheets in northern Canada and Greenland. When that ice shelf disappeared, it helped unlock part of these ice sheets, which contributed to hundreds of feet of sea level rise, establishing modern coastlines as we know them. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hearing laughter may cause orangutans to value rewards more
item.description: A new study from Indiana University shows that being in a positive mood leads orangutans to value what they learned more strongly. The study comes from the lab of Erica Cartmill, professor of animal behavior, anthropology and cognitive science in the College of Arts and Sciences at IU Bloomington, and was led by Daan Laméris, a postdoctoral researcher at IU. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: El Niño is threatening California's fragile coast again—the 1982–83 El Niño opened eyes to the serious erosion risks
item.description: California's coastal bluffs and beaches look rugged, but they can be surprisingly fragile in the face of a powerful El Niño. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Conducts RS-25 Engine Test in Support of Future Artemis Missions
item.description: NASA tested RS-25 engine No. 10001 on Oct. 21 on the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi. Test teams fired the developmental engine for almost eight-and-a-half minutes (500 seconds), the same amount of time RS-25 engines fire during launch of NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket. During […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: LaToya Dean

item.title: Japan's expensive funerals and declining birthrates are transforming ancestral traditions
item.description: Whenever I drive amid the mazelike bustle of Tokyo's Shuto Expressway, where approximately 1 million vehicles transit daily, I see billboard advertisements for all manner of businesses: dentists, hotels, car and tire companies, and affordable funerals. Lots and lots of funerals. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Salt marshes are proving to be powerful allies in building a climate-resilient coastline
item.description: Salt marsh sediment and vegetation can remain largely intact even during extreme storm surges. This was demonstrated in a large-scale experiment in which researchers transported sections of salt marsh to an experimental facility capable of producing the world's largest artificial waves. The results show how salt marshes can contribute to natural coastal protection, both in the Netherlands and beyond. The results were published in the journals Nature and Communications Sustainability. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Reconstructing 16,000 years of summer temperature change in the Western Balkans
item.description: Researchers at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE) have reconstructed approximately 16,000 years of summer temperature changes from sediments collected at Lake Prokoško in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The findings show how the Western Balkans responded to rapid climate changes at the end of the last glacial period, how warmer and cooler phases unfolded during the Holocene, and how the impact of human land use became increasingly pronounced. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI designs functional enzyme components that could help expand drug discovery
item.description: New active ingredients for drugs to treat infections, cancer or other serious diseases are often based on substances originally discovered in microorganisms, plants or other living organisms. Producing or improving such active ingredients in a targeted manner using microorganisms is often challenging because the underlying biological processes are extremely complex. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A scuff on your bag, a dent in your mug—and suddenly it feels like time for a new one
item.description: Imagine you have a bag you really like. It felt like "the one" when you bought it. Over time, it starts to look worn. There are some scuffs on it. Nothing is actually wrong with the bag, and it still works exactly as it should. Yet, once you notice those imperfections, you start thinking about buying a new one to replace it. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Snail shell rings could hold prehistoric cyclone information
item.description: Snail growth could be linked to extreme weather rather than annual patterns, enabling researchers to determine past cyclones. Fuente: ABC News Australia.
item.dc:creator: Nikki Sorbello and David Dowsett

item.title: Breaking through the 'fog of war': Game-based study suggests shared boundaries can foster peace
item.description: What causes adversaries to escalate conflicts into costly, prolonged wars even when neither side wants to fight? And in the fog of war, what might help them break that cycle and find a path to peace? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Using AI to plan your next vacation? Sometimes, too much information is just too much
item.description: Imagine planning a vacation across India's Golden Triangle: Delhi, Agra and Jaipur. You could compare dozens of websites, scroll through reviews and ask friends for recommendations. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What faces in paintings can tell us about how we perceive emotion
item.description: Look closely at a face in a painting and you might think you know what emotion the person is experiencing. A smile suggests happiness. A furrowed brow might signal anger. Widened eyes could mean fear or surprise. But what happens when you ask lots of people the same question? Do they see the same emotion, or something more complicated? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ancient fish bones reveal how Arctic cod species survived the last ice age
item.description: The glacial Arctic Ocean was not a barren ice desert but a breeding ground for the evolution of cold adaptation in marine fish. This is the main conclusion of a new scientific publication from Stockholm University that examines small fish bones found in deep-sea sediments during an expedition aboard the Swedish icebreaker Oden. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Genetic snapshot of North Carolina black bears could improve population resilience
item.description: A recent genomic survey of North Carolina black bears from mountain and coastal habitats reveals distinct differences in genetic health and diversity between the populations, with coastal bears exhibiting greater genetic fragility than mountain bears. The results could be used by wildlife management and law enforcement to ensure the health of both bears and the ecosystems they are part of. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Científicos convierten plástico en miles de millones de nanodiamantes mediante potentes disparos láser
item.description: Investigadores en Alemania han utilizado un láser de alta potencia para convertir una fina lámina de plástico en diamantes. Nanodiamantes, para ser más precisos, partículas que miden tan solo unos pocos milmillonésimos de metro de ancho. Lo interesante es que,por primera vez, han capturado estos nanodiamantes intactos y han podido examinarlos. No es que de repente podamos fabricarnos joyas con gigantescos pedruscos de diamantes, pero el hito es importante porque se podría convertir en la forma más limpia de fabricar nanodiamantes que ya se utilizan en la industria. Qué ha pasado . Un equipo… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Antonio Vallejo

item.title: Annual 'Teens and Screens' report reveals young audiences are redefining modern storytelling
item.description: The media habits of teens and young adults reflect transformative changes in modern storytelling and technology, and the entertainment industry and other content creators should pay attention, according to the latest "Teens and Screens" report from the Center for Scholars & Storytellers (CSS) at UCLA. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Swiss barn owls are gradually changing color
item.description: Over the past 30 years, Swiss barn owls have become more reddish-brown and more heavily spotted. By analyzing the genomes of more than 3,000 birds, scientists at the University of Lausanne identified the genetic variants linked to these changes in plumage and revealed natural selection at work. Their findings, published in Nature Communications, show that evolution can happen rapidly in the wild. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: X-ray free-electron laser sets new record for shortest high-energy pulses
item.description: Researchers at the Linac Coherent Light Source (LCLS) at the U.S. Department of Energy's SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory have measured the shortest high-energy X-ray pulses ever recorded at an X-ray free-electron laser (XFEL). The pulses had photon energies of about 9 kiloelectronvolts (keV) and clocked in at durations of 100 to 400 attoseconds—mere billionths of a billionth of a second. The results are published in Nature Photonics. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Study identifies world's first corporate psychopath
item.description: New research suggests the same personality traits associated with toxic corporate leaders today may have been present at the very birth of global capitalism 400 years ago. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA JPL Looks to Next 90 Years of Innovation, Exploration
item.description: Interstellar probes. Lunar drones. Helicopters on Mars. When a group of Caltech graduate students and enthusiasts began conducting rocket-propulsion tests in Pasadena’s Arroyo Seco on Oct. 31, 1936, they had no idea that their work marked the inception of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Ninety years later, the lab, now managed by Caltech for NASA, isn’t […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Barnett

item.title: NASA's CASALS instrument bridges gaps in 3D maps of Earth's surface
item.description: A team of researchers at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) has developed a new instrument designed to eliminate blind spots between lines of lidar data on Earth's surface. Built with support from NASA's Earth Science Technology Office (ESTO), the Concurrent Artificially-intelligent Spectrometry Lidar System (CASALS) could help researchers map the features of Earth's surface in detail. Rather than mechanically steering a laser with moving mirrors, CASALS steers light using wavelength itself, generating a continuous, 3D swath of the ground below. Publicado también por: NASA. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Butterfly navigation tests reveal that migrating species may rely on different natural compasses
item.description: Researchers at Keele University have discovered that migratory butterflies may use different navigation systems to find their way during migrations, highlighting the importance of understanding how different species may respond to environmental changes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hay tanta basura en órbita que los científicos proponen algo: que cada satélite pague una fianza de 200.000 dólares
item.description: ¿Sabes cuando continuamente pierdes la cartera, las llaves de casa y las gafas de sol, pero nunca pierdes de vista el mando del garaje porque has pagado una fianza de 50 euros? Un equipo de científicos de la Universidad de Colorado Boulder y el University College London quiere hacer algo parecido con los operadores de satélites, aunque en su propuesta no se trataría de no perder nada, sino de desorbitar los satélites para que no se conviertan en basura espacial. Si lo hacen, les devuelven con intereses una fianza de 200.000 dólares. Si no, ese dinero va a un fondo común para financiar medidas… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Azucena Martín

item.title: Scientists discover migration-mediated mechanism enabling bacteria-virus coexistence
item.description: Bacteria and the viruses that infect them—known as phages—coexist in soils, oceans and living organisms. Scientists have long thought this coexistence reflects a microscopic version of an evolutionary arms race: As parasites and hosts continually adapt to one another, both evolve ways to survive. But a joint study by researchers at the University of Maryland and the University of Exeter shows different pathways to coexistence. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Keeping to warm climates may have helped crocodiles outlast the dinosaurs
item.description: Keeping to warm climates throughout their 250-million-year history may have helped crocodiles and their relatives survive the asteroid that killed the dinosaurs, finds a new study led by UCL (University College London) researchers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Compulsive social media use is linked with wanting closeness but fearing reliance on others
item.description: Compulsive use of social media may be associated with a strong desire for reassurance among people who are afraid to rely on others and engage in face-to-face interactions, according to a study published Oct. 21, 2026, in the journal PLOS One by Chris Bjornsen and Allen Harbaugh of Longwood University in the U.S. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Electronic nose puts police detection dogs to the test
item.description: A pilot study tested an electronic nose, called NOS.E, alongside human-remains detection dogs to see whether it could detect buried remains and help confirm dogs' signals. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Forensic specialists need only one or two facial features to identify individuals
item.description: Researchers led by Carina Hahn at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), U.S., have found that forensic specialists in facial identification need only one or two features, such as eyes or ears, to identify a face when looking for a match. Published in PLOS One, the study found that specialists find ears to be the most useful but are capable of adapting when recognizing that another feature might be more beneficial. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Preschoolers aren't more creative than adults—they're just more confident
item.description: Adults are more objectively creative than preschoolers but are inhibited by anxiety and low self-confidence, according to a study published Oct. 21, 2026, in the journal PLOS One by Janika Saretzki from the University of Graz, Austria, and colleagues. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chromosome anchors form hollow shells before cell division, imaging reveals
item.description: Whenever a cell divides, it has to split its chromosomes perfectly between two daughter cells, and even a single mistake can be disastrous. Now, researchers from Japan have found that one of the key structures that makes this possible takes a surprising shape: a hollow sphere. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Silent' vultures turn out to use a wide range of sounds to communicate
item.description: Vultures were long thought to make few and fairly simple sounds. Yet no one had investigated in detail how the birds use sound to communicate. For his master's thesis in Jorg Massen's Vulture Cognition Lab, Connor Proudfoot studied the critically endangered Rüppell's vulture. He and his colleagues found that the birds produce a wide range of complex sounds, which they use in a range of social situations. The findings, published today in PLOS One, could help improve the success of captive breeding programs and shed light on the evolution of communication. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ukrainian media coverage casts land as both lifeline and danger zone
item.description: An international team led by Alexander Vorbrugg analyzed (online) media reporting on war-related land changes in Ukraine. The study asked: How is damage to land represented? What knowledge do these representations draw on? How does the war affect the symbolic meaning of land and visions of the future? How are material damage and destruction translated into the media discourse? What ideas of landscape does this create? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ultrafast light can control ferromagnetism without relying on heating
item.description: Despite being known for more mundane uses such as sticking notes to refrigerators or keeping bags shut, magnetization is one of the most fundamental and useful properties of a material. Indeed, it forms the physical basis for storing most of our digital information, encoding the bits used in hard drives, computer memories and credit cards. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Better data analysis links to stronger marketing and innovation in Thai retail sector
item.description: A study of 500 Thai retailers has found that businesses with stronger big data analytics capabilities tend to be better at identifying market needs, innovating and executing effective marketing strategies. Moreover, large retailers report higher capability levels than smaller firms, according to research published in the International Journal of Services and Operations Management. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: When a few people break the rules, bad behavior spreads quickly
item.description: The old saying that one bad apple spoils the barrel suggests that an individual behaving badly can have a negative influence on the entire group. The idea now has some fresh scientific backing. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Methane emissions in Baltimore show seasonal, daily trends
item.description: Natural gas leaks are a significant source of methane emissions in cities, but it can be hard to pinpoint exactly where and why they happen. And methane, a potent greenhouse gas that is the main chemical component of natural gas, has been historically undercounted or omitted in emissions estimates, according to a team of atmospheric and climate science researchers in the Penn State College of Earth and Mineral Sciences. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hubble observations challenge supernova winds' role in cosmic reionization
item.description: An international team of researchers, including members from the University of Michigan, has revealed surprising results that could rewrite our understanding of a key transition in the early universe. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Proposed additional ID requirements for voting could disenfranchise more than 1 in 4 Detroit adults
item.description: More than 1 in 4 Detroiters cannot easily produce up-to-date documentation of their U.S. citizenship that matches their current name, according to a new survey from the University of Michigan's Detroit Metro Area Communities Study, in partnership with Outlier Media. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Poor ocean conditions leave murrelet chicks exposed to nest predators for longer
item.description: Less favorable ocean conditions mean marbled murrelet chicks take longer to leave the nest, making them more vulnerable to predation, according to a new study of the Pacific Northwest seabird by Oregon State University scientists. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Childhood experiences of war loom large over CEOs' decision-making
item.description: The trauma of war has long-lasting reverberations, influencing business decisions made decades later, argue Eun Hye Jo and Jenny Jung-Wha Lee, accounting professors at Costello College of Business based at George Mason University Korea. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Two-in-one tool tracks viral RNA inside live infected cells in real time
item.description: Viruses are sneaky intruders, hijacking the internal machinery of host cells and replicating out of sight. Understanding these dynamics is the first step to developing effective antiviral strategies that could stop infections, but scientists have largely been left in the dark because there are limited tools to study how viruses move in space and time inside live infected cells, according to Joyce Jose, associate professor of biochemistry and molecular biology at Penn State. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Reindeer grazing changes plant roots in pine forests
item.description: Reindeer grazing changes the vegetation of northern pine forests below ground as well as above it. In a recent study in Finland, trees and understory vegetation in grazed forests had nearly 30% less shallow-root biomass than those in ungrazed areas. Root structure also changed, which may affect the ability of plants to take up water and nutrients. The research is published in the journal Oikos. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA to Conduct NCAA Flyover, Engage Fans at University of Alabama
item.description: As part of the agency’s Inspiration Tour, NASA will conduct a flyover at the University of Alabama vs. Texas A&M football game in Tuscaloosa, Alabama, on Saturday, Oct. 24. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman will pilot one of three F-5 fighter jets during the flyover, highlighting NASA’s contributions to aeronautics and the agency’s continued commitment to […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Lee Mohon

item.title: Migratory birds spread avian influenza to Greenland's polar bears
item.description: Migrating birds that breed in the Arctic are spreading avian influenza to polar bears in eastern Greenland, according to a new study that found evidence of infections in bear blood samples acquired from Greenland Inuit subsistence hunters. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Light-based method could offer first way to detect hypothetical 'mirror life'
item.description: Scientists have proposed what they believe is the first method for detecting "mirror life"—a hypothetical form of life made from molecular building blocks that are the mirror image of those found naturally on Earth. Researchers at the University of Strathclyde and the Department of Chemistry at Durham University have outlined a new approach that could identify mirror organisms using molecules which emit left- and right-handed light. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: “Talent in, Impact Out”: Inside The Education University of Hong Kong's vision for an interconnected world of talent and expertise
item.description: [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] The Education University of Hong Kong (EdUHK) pursues a dual internationalisation strategy: attracting talented students, scholars and researchers from around the world while exporting educational and research expertise to communities beyond Hong Kong. “We live in an interconnected world that goes beyond the West, and it should be viewed as a highly connected whole,” says EdUHK President Professor John Lee Chi-Kin.... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Advertising partner

item.title: South Korea guides crowd-pulling shark out of canal
item.description: A shark that has become a viral sensation in South Korea was coaxed out of a canal in which it was stuck, authorities said on Wednesday, as falling temperatures raised concerns for its survival. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tracks Along the Longest Drive on Another World
item.description: Written by Vandi Verma, Chief Engineer for Robotic Operations at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory Oct. 12, 2026 Since the last blog update, Perseverance has achieved a major milestone on Mars. On Sol 2006 (Oct. 11, 2026), its odometer reached 45.22 kilometers (28.10 miles), setting a new record for the farthest distance driven on another celestial […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Mirror-image molecules are difficult to separate from their counterparts, but a new catalytic method might be the answer
item.description: Just like gloves, molecules can have left- and right-handed—or mirror-image—forms. Because the left- and right-handed molecules are still very similar, scientists have had trouble separating them from each other. But a team of researchers in Japan might have found a solution. In their new study, published in Science Advances, the team successfully separated an equal mixture of mirror-image molecules created by replacing hydrogen with deuterium in one form. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Invisible' tweak could help make protein shakes less clumpy
item.description: Scientists from RMIT University and Riga Technical University in Latvia have shown that static charge left on surfaces can be controlled, which may have big benefits for companies needing to avoid the little zap in production of common household goods. The discovery could even one day help stop powders such as protein, chocolate malt powders and coffee from clumping. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Science on the Space Station with NASA Astronaut Jessica Watkins
item.description: NASA astronaut and Expedition 75 flight engineer Jessica Watkins works inside the Kibo laboratory module’s Life Science Glovebox on Oct. 9, 2026, safely mixing living cell samples with a bioink and then filling a special cartridge with the cell‑ink mixture. The advanced research operations were part of the InSPA‑Auxilium Bioprinter‑Cell Printing investigation, which explores 3D […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Beyond infections, bacteria reveal promise for making medicines and protecting crops
item.description: Bacteria get a bad reputation—with all the outbreaks, infections and deaths. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Burnham and Badenoch clash over Jackdaw gasfield as Trump welcomes decision – UK politics live
item.description: The Jackdaw field will start supplying gas to homes and businesses from the end of the month, the government said Here is an explainer by Jill Ambrose about the Jackdaw decision. But environmental groups have condemned the decision. Ami McCarthy, head of politics for Greenpeace UK , said: Approving Jackdaw shows the toxic grip fossil fuel lobbyists still hold over our energy policy. Andy Burnham promised pragmatism [see 8.40am ] , but there is nothing pragmatic about rubber-stamping a project that won’t lower energy bills, won’t boost energy security and will create just 27 full-time jobs …… Publicado también por: The Guardian - Environment. Fuente: The Guardian - World.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Sparrow

item.title: Massive study of 460,000 people challenges ultra-processed food cancer fears
item.description: A massive study of more than 460,000 Americans found that ultra-processed foods were not associated with increased colorectal cancer risk overall, challenging a widely held assumption. While processed meat was linked to higher cancer incidence, ultra-processed whole grains and dairy products were associated with lower incidence. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Astronomers uncover the engine behind the most powerful stellar flares in the Kepler field
item.description: A new study led by researchers at the Konkoly Observatory of the HUN-REN Research Centre for Astronomy and Earth Sciences (HUN-REN CSFK) in Budapest has revealed what makes a distant red giant star the most explosively active in the entire Kepler field—and the answer lies in a surprisingly subtle interplay between a close stellar companion, vast dark starspots and a highly efficient internal magnetic dynamo. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Australia urged to put biodiversity at the heart of planning as global targets slip out of reach
item.description: The world is falling short of its biodiversity commitments because nature is still treated as an afterthought in decisions about housing, infrastructure, agriculture, energy, mining and conservation, according to a new UNSW report. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Too much RNA can starve cells of energy, scientists discover
item.description: Scientists have uncovered an unexpected danger lurking inside cells: too much RNA can damage the structures responsible for producing energy. A new study found that excess RNA, including the normally essential messenger RNA (mRNA), can directly disrupt mitochondria without relying on the immune system. The discovery could help explain how viral infections and certain aging-related diseases damage cells. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

Tenemos problemas para reproducir este vídeo. Más información Ver más comentarios Freda Edwards Fuente: National Geographic.

item.title: AI reveals how a warming climate will intensify NZ's most extreme downpours
item.description: The most damaging weather events are the record-breaking "one-in-100-year" disasters communities have usually only seen once. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The ocean's most abundant 'loner' microbe has a sticky second life
item.description: The oxygen in about every other breath we take comes from microscopic cells—phytoplankton—drifting in the surface of the ocean. Among them is Prochlorococcus, the smallest and most abundant photosynthetic organism in the seas. It single-handedly accounts for roughly 10% of all the carbon that the land and the oceans pull from the atmosphere each year. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tackling Lake Erie's algal blooms requires targeted conservation strategies
item.description: Anyone living along the coast of Lake Erie will be well aware of the periodic algal blooms that appear on its surface. The greenish blooms can cause rashes and other health problems and pose risks to both humans and animals. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A train was delayed by a solar storm. But something didn't add up.
item.description: Scientists have cracked a 178-year-old mystery surrounding a train delayed by a solar storm, revealing that the famous incident happened in 1848 rather than 1841. The discovery rewrites the early history of space weather and highlights a threat that still endangers modern power grids, satellites, and communication systems. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Genomes of 20 eastern Finnish species provide unique insights into species' adaptations to local conditions
item.description: In recent years, researchers at the University of Eastern Finland have been both leading and contributing to collaborative genome projects. These efforts have produced reference-quality genome assemblies for the Finnish brown hare and the mountain hare, as well as the Saimaa ringed seal, in collaboration with research partners. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA’s CASALS Instrument Bridges Gaps in 3D Maps of Earth’s Surface
item.description: From orbit, today’s space-based laser instruments measure Earth’s forests and terrain one narrow line at a time. Between those lines are enormous gaps that include millions of acres of land scientists never directly measure. NASA’s CASALS instrument will blend machine learning with an ultra-compact lidar instrument to adaptively ‘sweep’ large swaths of Earth’s surface. This […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: FOSSA Systems e IENAI Space han puesto en órbita el primer satélite español con propulsión eléctrica
item.description: Este 20 de octubre de 2026 se ha lanzado un satélite 6U desde Cabo Cañaveral, Florida, a bordo de un cohete Falcon 9, de SpaceX. El lanzamiento, que forma parte de la misión compartida Bandwagon-5, ha sido todo un hito español, ya que es el primer satélite de propulsión eléctrica de fabricación española. Más español que la paella . El satélite ha sido fabricado por la compañía española Fossa Systems . Es el número 27 que se lanza desde 2020; por lo que, según comunicados recogidos por Actualidad Aeroespacial , sería ya la empresa de España que más objetos ha puesto en órbita. En cuanto a sus… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Azucena Martín

item.title: Parents and nongamers struggle to identify video game loot boxes
item.description: New research has found parents, guardians and nongamers may struggle to recognize video game loot boxes, their defining features and the digital receipts linked to purchases. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Astronauts’ hearts just passed a surprising test for Mars
item.description: A new study tracking 13 astronauts suggests that the human heart may be surprisingly well equipped for a journey to Mars, especially with regular exercise during spaceflight. Researchers found that astronauts' hearts adapted to months of weightlessness and handled simulated Martian gravity without major problems, offering new hope for future missions to the Red Planet. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Atomic memory keeps distant ions entangled for about 10 seconds
item.description: Quantum networks, systems that connect devices and allow them to exchange information encoded in the quantum states of particles, could enable more secure communications. To build these networks, physicists need to devise strategies that allow distant particles to share quantum states, preserving them long enough to perform calculations or enable communication between devices. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Can surplus-food apps have too much competition?
item.description: Apps that let businesses sell surplus food at a discount in "surplus bags" have become a popular way to keep edible food out of landfills while giving consumers access to lower-cost meals and groceries. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rejuvenation breakthrough: Scientists reverse 60 years of aging in human cells
item.description: Scientists have turned blood cells from an 80-year-old into neural stem cells with a molecular age of less than 20, effectively reversing more than 60 years of cellular aging in the laboratory. The discovery offers a new way to investigate how cells become younger and could help researchers better understand age-related diseases such as Alzheimer's. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Q&A: Do new platform features hurt hiring chances for competitive gig workers?
item.description: Whether they are driven by economic necessity or a desire for greater control over their careers, a growing number of workers are turning to online gig-work platforms to supplement their income with freelance projects like coding or website design. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Synchronized bodily responses do not always reflect cooperation, study finds
item.description: Sometimes, while people are interacting with each other, their movements and physiological responses can fall into step. Some past studies have linked synchronized bodily responses to cooperation and being attuned to the emotions of others. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Musk talks up potential merger of SpaceX and Tesla
item.description: As SpaceX reports blockbuster quarterly earnings, CEO Elon Musk floats the possibility of merging the rocketry and AI firm with his electric car company Tesla. Also in this edition: OpenAI reveals more agent misbehaviour as market turmoil hits data centre companies, and France's political crisis exacerbates its bond market rout. Fuente: France 24 - English.

item.title: ‘Jackdaw means we pay our mortgages’: relief in Aberdeen over gasfield approval
item.description: Few believe decision will bring back city’s boom years, but workers hope it will secure North Sea jobs for now UK approves Jackdaw gasfield in North Sea What does the UK’s approval of the Jackdaw gasfield mean? As recently as 2012, Aberdeen boasted the highest concentration of millionaires in the UK. An ATM reportedly had the highest withdrawal rate in Europe in the 90s, as oil and gas wealth flowed through the city. House prices skyrocketed in the scramble for space as fossil fuel firms transformed the city’s grand granite houses into company offices. But that was then. Today, “for sale” and… Fuente: The Guardian - Environment.
item.dc:creator: Patrick Greenfield

item.title: Just 4 minutes a day can dramatically improve strength after 65
item.description: A new Penn State study suggests that just four minutes of daily strength training can significantly improve mobility and physical function in older adults. After 12 weeks, participants showed meaningful gains in balance, leg strength, and their ability to stand up from a chair, all important factors for maintaining independence and reducing fall risk. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: South Korea launches new bid to guide crowd-pulling shark to sea
item.description: South Korean authorities began a new attempt Wednesday to coax a shark-turned-viral sensation back to sea, with falling temperatures in the Busan canal where it is stranded raising concerns for its survival. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover just shattered the all-time off-world driving record
item.description: NASA’s Perseverance rover has shattered a historic space exploration record, traveling farther across another world than any vehicle before it. Its advanced self-driving system helped it surpass Opportunity’s 28.06-mile record in just five and a half years, a feat that previously took nearly 15. Now, Perseverance is exploring some of the oldest rocks in the solar system, searching for clues about ancient Martian environments that may once have supported life. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Prized wild pepper at risk in Madagascar's shrinking forests
item.description: A rare wild pepper endemic to Madagascar and prized by international chefs is facing an uncertain future, a victim of its own success and the destruction of its forest habitat. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: More current with less calcium: Computational models help solve longstanding ion channel evolution mystery
item.description: In the early 1980s, scientists observed an anomaly. Embedded within cell membranes, they identified ion channels with extraordinarily high conductance. These so-called "BK" (Big K, or Big Potassium) channels had roughly 10 times the unitary conductance (i.e., conductance per individual channel molecule) of other potassium channels, enabling much more efficient, rapid transport of potassium ions. And while later structural characterization explained how this happened, no one could understand why. That is, until now. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Transparent minispheres reveal that some look-alike cancer drugs part ways in 3D
item.description: Researchers at Uppsala University have adapted Cell Painting, a widely used imaging method in drug discovery, to look at individual cells inside small 3D clusters of cancer cells. Two drugs that looked almost identical in ordinary flat cell cultures behaved differently in 3D, and the team linked the difference to how each drug switches on the cell's p53 stress response. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A First Nation community in Canada is using a data center to preserve its heritage
item.description: For thousands of years, Indigenous peoples have passed down their traditions and culture through oral storytelling. Now, a Canadian Indigenous community is using a data center to help preserve its heritage. Publicado también por: The Hindu - International. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: SpaceX turns a profit after a string of losses as its satellite and computer leasing businesses soar
item.description: SpaceX reported a bigger quarterly profit than expected Tuesday as its satellite communications operations and its business of leasing computing power to other companies boomed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: The Labour administration promised when returning to power in 2024 not to issue any new oil and gas drilling licences as it steers Britain away from fossil fuels towards cleaner renewable energy. Fuente: The Hindu - International.

item.title: Targeting a particular gene may improve tea plants' flavor and cold tolerance
item.description: Research in New Phytologist reveals a gene that regulates tea plants' flavor and cold tolerance, providing insights on how to expand the potential for better-tasting tea to be grown in a wider variety of locations. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: U.S. antipoverty tax credit expansion may have unintended costs for children's development
item.description: As part of U.S. welfare reforms in the 1990s to provide adequate financial support to low-income families while avoiding disincentivizing work, policymakers expanded the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC). This change encouraged people to work more by giving greater benefits with greater earned income, and single mothers faced stronger incentives to enter the workforce than married mothers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A massive asteroid slammed into the North Sea and unleashed a 330-foot tsunami
item.description: A decades-long mystery beneath the North Sea has finally been solved. Scientists have confirmed that the Silverpit Crater, buried 700 meters below the seabed, was created when a 160-meter-wide asteroid struck Earth roughly 43 to 46 million years ago. The violent collision blasted a towering curtain of rock and water 1.5 kilometers into the air and triggered a tsunami more than 100 meters high. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: China builds the world’s smallest wearable brain monitor with a cortex-wide view
item.description: Chinese scientists have developed what they say is the world’s smallest wearable mini brain monitor that can track the activity of thousands of neurons at the same time. Weighing in at one gram (0.35 oz), the wireless “Airscope” is the lightest device of its kind and enables researchers to track a wider range of brain activity in untethered laboratory animals. The device was jointly developed by scientists from Tsinghua University and the Chinese PLA Medical School, and detailed in a paper... Fuente: South China Morning Post.

item.title: Guatemala gains its first endemic bird in American Ornithological Society's 67th supplement
item.description: The 67th Supplement to the American Ornithological Society's (AOS's) Check-list of North American Birds, which was published today in Ornithology, includes several significant updates to the classification of bird species found in North America, Central America and the Caribbean. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover ghostly, eyeless creature hidden in Chinese cave
item.description: Deep inside a high-altitude Chinese cave, scientists discovered a ghostly, eyeless freshwater snail that has evolved to live entirely in darkness, marking the first recorded discovery of its kind in China. Named after a faceless mythical creature, the rare species may already be in danger, with researchers finding only three living adults. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: A magnetar can be born when two neutron stars touch
item.description: All neutron stars have intense magnetic fields. The typical magnetic field of a neutron star is about 100,000 times stronger than the strongest magnetic fields we can create on Earth. But about 1% of neutron stars have even stronger magnetic fields. Known as magnetars, their magnetic fields can be 1,000 times stronger than a regular magnetic field. They are a likely cause of powerful transient events such as soft gamma-ray repeaters and fast radio bursts. A new study looks at how magnetars might form. The findings are published on the arXiv preprint server. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Women farmers need better financing to benefit from AI
item.description: Public and private investments must address the financial barriers preventing women from benefiting fully from digital technologies and artificial intelligence as multiple global crises and aid cuts bite. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Are partisan politics even changing up our accents? They just might be, y'all
item.description: With the midterms fast approaching, communicating just the right message has been top of mind on all sides of the political aisle. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists find 10 different diets linked to slower aging
item.description: A study by DZNE finds that healthy eating is associated with slower biological aging—and that there is more than one way to eat healthily. The researchers examined ten dietary patterns considered healthy, including the Mediterranean, Nordic, and a plant-based diet, as well as the DASH diet, which is designed to help lower blood pressure. The findings are published in the journal Nature Communications. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Controlled vapor treatment guides molecules into highly oriented soft quasicrystals
item.description: Molecules can spontaneously organize into complex, ordered structures through a process known as self-assembly. Among these structures, soft quasicrystals display unusual patterns that do not repeat regularly like conventional crystals. However, producing such structures with a uniform orientation over large areas remains a major challenge. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Major repairs needed to save Horseshoe Bay Lagoon
item.description: Volunteer researcher Chris Hopper, JCU's adjunct professor Eric Wolanski and independent researcher Natalie K. Dowling examined the impact of saltwater and erosion on Horseshoe Bay Lagoon, a freshwater lagoon and one of the few swamps with bulkuru sedge—also known as water chestnut—on the Magnetic Island (Yunbenun). The study is published in the journal Applied Sciences. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rare solar radiation storm gives scientists clearest picture yet of flight risks
item.description: The most comprehensive data set ever collected from Earth's atmosphere during a solar radiation event has highlighted the importance of better-coordinated radiation monitoring for aviation safety, according to new research led by the University of Surrey. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Shortening Canadian teacher education risks devaluing the profession of teaching
item.description: Recently, shorter teacher certification programs have been introduced in different Canadian provinces. These programs are being implemented in Alberta, Nova Scotia, Ontario and Québec. Fuente: Phys.org.
